episodes.title: The Next Trillion Internet Users Still Don’t Have an Identity — Adi Singh, AgentMail
episodes.description:
Adi Singh let an agent run unsupervised to recruit other agents. It started calling itself a prophet of persistent identity.

NEXT UP: AI ENGINEER CODE SUMMIT
Join us in SF for the second annual AIE CODE Summit, Nov 10–12, our last flagship summit of 2026. Applications live now: https://aie.codes

Adi Singh, co-founder of AgentMail, argues that agent identity won't be issued by a new spec but accumulated on the surfaces humans already use, like email, the way MCP spread by bringing tools to apps people already lived in. He shares what happened when he let an agent run unsupervised to sign up other agents, explains why existing surfaces are both a trust surface and an attack surface, and walks through Telnyx's autonomous agent signup, where an AgentMail inbox lets an agent verify itself, get an API key and stay reachable for billing and support. He closes with what will break as agent numbers grow.

In this video:
- Why identity is accumulated, not issued
- How MCP spread by bringing tools to existing surfaces
- Trust vs attack surface: email's strengths and risks for agents
- A real autonomous agent signup flow with Telnyx

episodes.title: Decoupling the Brain from the Hands: Claude Managed Agents (Part 1 of 4) — Anthropic
episodes.description:
The first version of Claude Managed Agents put everything in one container. Here's why Anthropic split it apart.

NEXT UP: AI ENGINEER CODE SUMMIT
Join us in SF for the second annual AIE CODE Summit, Nov 10–12, our last flagship summit of 2026. Applications live now: https://aie.codes

Priyanka Phatak, who leads the Claude Managed Agents engineering team at Anthropic, defines an agent as a model in a loop with tools, plus a harness and a sandbox, and explains why harnesses encode assumptions that go stale with each new model. She walks through the first architecture, where the session, harness and sandbox shared one hard-to-debug 'pet' container, and the redesign into an append-only session log, a brain (harness plus Claude) and hands (sandboxes and tools). Credentials stay out of the sandbox and time to first token dropped about 90%. Then she introduces the core APIs with a simple joke-teller agent.

This is part 1 of 4 of the Claude Managed Agents workshop from Anthropic.

In this video:
• Why harnesses carry model-specific assumptions
• Decoupling session, harness and sandbox into replaceable parts
• Injecting credentials at an egress proxy so Claude never sees them
• The core flow: environment, agent, session, events

episodes.title: Auth for Agents: Let AI Sign Up for Your Product with auth.md — Michael Grinich, WorkOS
episodes.description:
Agents are starting to pick your vendors, and most signup flows block them at the door.

NEXT UP: AI ENGINEER CODE SUMMIT
Join us in SF for the second annual AIE CODE Summit, Nov 10–12, our last flagship summit of 2026. Applications live now: https://aie.codes

Michael Grinich, founder and CEO of WorkOS, argues that as agents run for hours and increasingly choose tools on their own, services have to make something agents want. The missing piece is agent registration: today's signup flows assume a human who can fill out forms, solve CAPTCHAs and copy API keys, and MCP auth still needs a person in the loop. He introduces auth.md, an open spec built on OAuth standards that tells agents how to register, then demos an agent that finds Cloudflare's auth.md, proves its identity with ID-JAG, gets a temporary account and deploys an app with no human signup.

In this video:
• Why login boxes and CAPTCHAs block legitimate agents
• What an auth.md file declares for agent signup

episodes.title: Stop Renting Intelligence: The Train-to-Deploy Loop for Specialized AI — Fireworks AI
episodes.description:
Closed models are getting expensive fast. Open models can match them, if you keep training them on your own data.

Jetashree Ravi, who leads part of the applied machine learning team at Fireworks AI, explains how teams move from closed models to open ones without losing quality. Her three truths: open models like GLM 5.2 are production-ready, customization closes the remaining quality gap, and the AI stack is shifting to a continuous train-and-serve loop. She shares Fireworks' scale (about 30 trillion tokens, 10,000+ companies) and customer results: Cursor's Composer 2 trained and hosted on Fireworks with 13x faster inference, a 40x latency improvement for Vercel, and 12% better quality for Genspark with reinforcement fine-tuning. She covers the FireAttention engine and its custom CUDA kernels, speculative decoding with custom draft models, and three ways to train (a training agent, managed training, and a training API for SFT, RFT and DPO), then the flywheel: one-click deploys, monitoring, hot-loading new weights with no downtime, and matching numerics between training and serving. She ends with demos of the training agent and managed training.

In this talk:
• Why open models plus customization can match closed ones
• FireAttention, custom kernels and speculative decoding
• Training agent, managed training and the training API
• Hot loading and numerical fidelity for a continuous train-and-deploy loop

episodes.title: Hill-Climbing Skills: Improve Agents Without Changing the Model — Shubhankar Srivastava, Browserbase
episodes.description:
An agent succeeds at a flight search, then fails on its next iteration. Shubhankar Srivastava uses that uneven progress to show how browser agents can learn a task without changing model weights. His AutoBrowse loop pairs a doer that operates the browser with a teacher that reads screenshots, traces and results after each run. The teacher writes lessons into a strategy file, and the next attempt starts with those lessons instead of starting from zero. The flight demo discovers that a URL can encode the search directly, avoiding repeated calendar clicks and an awkward time filter.

The final artifact is a skill file that future agents can reuse. Earlier runs on a conference schedule and restaurant search show how the file preserves navigation choices, waiting behavior and site specific constraints, while replays make the claimed results inspectable. Srivastava then explains what another domain would need to use the same approach: an environment that can be replayed and an outcome that can be verified. Questions expose the limits of that requirement, especially when finding an acceptable flight is easier to judge than finding the best one. The discussion explores task specific versus general skills, different optimization goals, iteration costs and how to measure the verifier itself. For changing websites, he describes monitoring and failure triggered repair loops that produce changes for human review. Prompt injection adds another constraint: generated skills need scrutiny alongside controls on inputs, allowed actions and destinations.
